title: Biggest Husqvarna Chainsaw: 3120 XP and the Big Pro Saws
h1: The Biggest Husqvarna Chainsaw, and the Lightest
meta: The biggest Husqvarna chainsaw is the 3120 XP at 118.8 cc. See how it compares with the 395XP, 592XP, 572XP and 372XP, plus the lightest Husqvarna saws.
dek: Which is the biggest Husqvarna chainsaw, who actually needs one, and the big pro saws and light top-handles most tree crews run instead.

sections.h: What is the biggest Husqvarna chainsaw?
p: The biggest Husqvarna chainsaw is the 3120 XP. At 118.8 cc it is the largest and most powerful saw in Husqvarna's professional lineup, rated at about 8.4 hp (6.2 kW), and the power head alone weighs about 22.9 lb before you add a bar and chain. It is usually sold as a power head only, so you choose the bar and chain to suit the work.

Below the 3120 XP sits a group of large professional saws in the 90 cc class, then the 70 cc saws that most removal crews treat as their everyday big saw. At the other end of the range are the small top-handle saws climbers carry in the tree, which are the lightest Husqvarna chainsaws you can buy.

This guide works down the range from largest to lightest, with the figures we are confident of, and explains which size makes sense for real tree work. For full details on any model, see the product pages in our chainsaws section.
list: Husqvarna 3120 XP: 118.8 cc, the largest and most powerful
Husqvarna 395XP: 93.6 cc, classic carbureted big saw
Husqvarna 592XP: 92.7 cc, newer big saw with AutoTune
Husqvarna 390XP: 88 cc, a lighter big-saw option
Husqvarna 572XP and 372XP: about 70 cc, the removal-crew workhorses
Husqvarna T525: 27 cc, the lightest gas top-handle

sections.h: Husqvarna 3120 XP: who needs a 120 cc saw
p: The Husqvarna 3120 XP is built for very large wood: felling and bucking big-diameter trunks, slabbing with a chainsaw mill, and cutting wide stumps and butt logs that a 90 cc saw would labor through. It pulls long bars that smaller saws cannot keep up with, and it is a common choice for chainsaw milling because it holds speed in a long, wide cut.

For most tree services it is a specialty saw, not a daily one. A 3120 XP with a long bar is heavy to carry across a yard and tiring to hold in a bucking position all day. Crews that own one tend to bring it out for the biggest removals, storm work on old trees and milling jobs, and leave it on the truck the rest of the time.

Big saws like this use a decompression valve to make starting manageable. Many owners run .404 chain on longer bars for durability in big wood, though 3/8 in chain is also used depending on the bar setup. Check the operator's manual for the bar and chain combinations Husqvarna approves for the saw.

For crews that regularly cut large wood but do not need a 120 cc saw, the 90 cc class is the sweet spot. The 395XP is the classic choice: 93.6 cc, about 6.6 hp, a conventional carburetor and a long track record on felling and bucking jobs. It is heavy, simple and strong, and a lot of saw hands still prefer it.

The 592XP is Husqvarna's newer saw in this class. At 92.7 cc it is rated at about 7.5 hp, and it uses AutoTune to manage the fuel mixture as conditions change. On paper and in the cut it is the more powerful of the two, and it is the one to look at if you want a modern big saw that several people can share without retuning.

The 390XP, at 88 cc, is a little lighter and was popular as a big saw that is still reasonable to carry. Husqvarna's 585 is another large professional saw a step below the 592XP. Availability of the older carbureted models varies by market, so check what is currently sold and supported where you work.

sections.h: 572XP and 372XP: the size most crews actually use
p: If you asked a room of removal climbers and ground crew which Husqvarna they reach for first, most would name a 70 cc saw. The 572XP (70.6 cc, AutoTune) and the older 372XP (70.7 cc, carbureted) have enough power to run an 18 to 28 inch bar for felling and bucking, and they are light enough to carry around a job and handle while blocking down a spar.

These saws are not the biggest Husqvarna chainsaws, but they cover the large majority of residential removal work. A crew with one 70 cc saw and one 90 cc or larger saw can handle almost anything that comes up. We compare the two in detail in our Husqvarna 372XP vs 572XP guide.

At the other end of the range, the lightest gas Husqvarna chainsaw is the T525 top-handle. It is a 27 cc saw that weighs about 5.9 lb as a power head and runs a 10 or 12 inch bar. It is built for pruning and light limb work aloft, where every ounce on the saddle matters.

Most production climbers step up to the T540XP, which has a 37.7 cc engine and runs a 12 to 16 inch bar, for more cutting speed on removals. Husqvarna also makes battery top-handle saws such as the T540i XP, which are quiet and start instantly, at the cost of carrying and charging batteries.
Top-handle saws are designed for trained arborists working in trees, not for general ground use. On the ground, run a rear-handle saw with both hands on the handles.

sections.h: Bars, chain and fuel for big saws
p: Bar length is where big saws earn their keep. A 90 cc or larger saw can pull a long bar through hardwood, but every inch of bar adds weight and makes the saw more front-heavy. Many crews keep a long bar for felling and big rounds and a shorter one for everyday bucking on the same power head.

Match pitch and gauge across your bars, chain and sprockets, and keep the oiler adjusted so a long bar gets enough oil. Our bars and chain section covers common setups. Run fresh fuel at the ratio in the manual, keep the air filter clean, and check the decompression valve and spark plug at regular service intervals.

sections.h: How to choose the right size Husqvarna
p: Buy for the wood you cut every week, not the biggest tree you might see once a year. A saw that is too large wears you out and costs more in fuel, bars and chain. A saw that is too small burns time in big wood and gets overworked. For many tree services the right setup is a top-handle for the climber, a 50 to 60 cc saw for limbing and brush, a 70 cc saw for removals, and a 90 cc or larger saw for the largest trees.

Whatever size you run, wear chainsaw pants or chaps, a helmet with eye and hearing protection, gloves and boots, and get proper chainsaw and felling training. A big saw with a long bar has more kickback energy and is harder to control, so it rewards good technique and punishes bad habits.

faq.q: What is the biggest Husqvarna chainsaw?
faq.a: The Husqvarna 3120 XP. It has a 118.8 cc engine rated at about 8.4 hp and is the largest saw in Husqvarna's professional lineup.

faq.q: What is the most powerful Husqvarna chainsaw?
faq.a: The 3120 XP is also the most powerful. Below it, the 592XP is rated at about 7.5 hp and the 395XP at about 6.6 hp.

faq.q: What is the lightest Husqvarna chainsaw?
faq.a: Among gas saws, the T525 top-handle is the lightest, at about 5.9 lb for the power head. It is intended for trained arborists working in trees.

faq.q: Does the Husqvarna 3120 XP come with a bar and chain?
faq.a: It is commonly sold as a power head only, so you add a bar and chain. Check the operator's manual for the approved bar lengths and chain types.

title: Longest Gas Pole Saw: Reach, Models and Safety
h1: Longest Gas Pole Saw: How Much Reach You Really Get
meta: Looking for the longest gas pole saw? How reach is measured, telescoping gas vs battery vs manual poles, the Husqvarna pole saws, and power line safety rules.
dek: What the longest gas pole saw can actually reach, when a manual pole goes higher, and how to stay safe working overhead.

sections.h: What makes the longest gas pole saw
p: When people search for the longest gas pole saw, they usually want to cut limbs as high as possible from the ground without a ladder, a climb or a lift. The answer depends on two numbers that are easy to confuse: the tool's overall length, and the working reach you get once you hold it.

Overall length is the measurement from the end of the handle to the tip of the bar, with the shaft fully extended on a telescoping model. Working reach adds your own height and arm position. Manufacturers often quote a reach figure that assumes you are holding the saw at a steep angle, so treat it as a best case. In practice you rarely cut straight overhead, and every degree you lean the pole out costs you height.

The longest gas pole saws are telescoping professional models. They give the most reach of any powered pole saw, but they also put a heavy engine at one end and a cutting head at the other, which makes them tiring to hold fully extended.

A telescoping gas pole saw lets you collapse the shaft for transport and low limbs, then extend it for high work. The Husqvarna 525PT5S is a common professional choice: a 25.4 cc X-Torq engine, a 12 inch bar and a telescoping shaft, built for crews that prune and clear all day.

When you compare models, look at extended length, weight, how the shaft locks, and how far the engine sits from your hands. A saw that balances well is easier to hold steady at full extension, which matters more than a few extra inches on the spec sheet. Also check the bar and chain size, since replacement pole saw chain is a regular expense.
Gas pole saws handle thicker limbs and long days without battery swaps. The trade-offs are noise, fuel mixing and more maintenance than a battery saw.

Husqvarna makes several pole saws that come up in searches for an extendable Husqvarna polesaw. The 525PT5S is the gas telescoping model. The 530iPT5 is the telescoping battery version; we list it as the Husqvarna 530iPT, sold as a tool only with a 10 inch bar on Husqvarna's 36V battery system.

For utility line clearance there is the Husqvarna MadSaw, a gas pole saw with a dielectric fiberglass shaft. It is a specialty tool for qualified line-clearance crews, not a homeowner upgrade. Some combi trimmers also accept a pole saw attachment, which is a good fit if you already own a split-shaft power head; see our Husqvarna 330LK vs 525L guide.

sections.h: Manual poles reach higher than any gas pole saw
p: If maximum reach is the goal, a manual pole saw beats a powered one. Without an engine on the end, sectional and telescoping poles can be built much longer and still be controlled. Arborists commonly stack fiberglass sections to reach well past what any gas pole saw offers.

Telescoping manual poles such as the Notch Nobasu 20 ft polesaw or the Jameson telescoping poles extend quickly and pack small. Sectional fiberglass poles let you add exactly the length you need. A sharp pull-stroke pole saw blade cuts surprisingly fast, and a pole pruner handles small clean cuts. Browse our poles and kits for options.

The trade-off is effort and diameter. A manual pole saw is slow on thick limbs, and the higher you go the harder it is to make a clean cut. Many crews carry both: a manual pole for reach and finish work, and a powered pole saw for volume.

Battery pole saws are quieter, start instantly and need less maintenance. They suit residential pruning, noise-sensitive jobs and crews that already run a battery platform. Reach is similar to gas models in the same class, and run time depends on the battery size and the wood you are cutting.
For all-day production pruning in thick limbs, a gas pole saw still has the edge. For shorter jobs and finish work, many crews find a battery pole saw is the one that gets used most.

sections.h: Power lines: the rule that matters most
p: Most pole saws are not insulated, and even a dry wooden or fiberglass pole can conduct electricity if it is dirty, wet or damaged. Unless you are a qualified line-clearance arborist, keep yourself, the pole saw and any branch you are cutting at least 10 feet from overhead lines, and more for higher-voltage lines. The limb you cut can also fall into a line.

If a tree is near power lines, call the utility or a qualified line-clearance tree company. Dielectric tools like the MadSaw are rated and tested for line work, but they are only safe in the hands of trained, qualified workers following line-clearance procedures under ANSI Z133 and OSHA rules.

sections.h: Using a long pole saw safely
p: Stand to the side of the limb, never directly under it, and plan where the piece will fall before you start. Wear a helmet, eye protection and gloves, plus hearing protection with a powered saw. Make a small undercut first on larger limbs so the bark does not tear down the stem, then finish from the top.
Do not use a pole saw from a ladder, and keep other people well clear of the drop zone. Keep the chain or blade sharp so you are not forcing the cut at full extension.
list: Check for power lines before every cut
Stand to the side, not under the limb
Undercut larger limbs to prevent bark tearing
Wear a helmet, eye protection and gloves
Keep bystanders out of the drop zone

faq.q: What is the longest gas pole saw?
faq.a: The longest gas pole saws are professional telescoping models. Compare each maker's extended length and listed reach, and remember that reach figures assume a steep working angle.

faq.q: Is the Husqvarna pole saw extendable?
faq.a: Yes. The 525PT5S gas pole saw and the 530iPT5 battery pole saw both have telescoping shafts.

faq.q: What reaches higher, a gas pole saw or a manual pole saw?
faq.a: A manual pole saw. Without an engine on the end, sectional or telescoping poles can be made longer and still be controlled.

faq.q: Can I use a pole saw near power lines?
faq.a: Not unless you are a qualified line-clearance arborist. Everyone else should keep themselves, the tool and the branch at least 10 feet from overhead lines and call the utility.

title: Rope Puller for Tree Felling: Pullers, Winches and Kits
h1: Choosing a Rope Puller for Tree Felling
meta: How to choose a rope puller for tree felling: endless rope pullers, rope come alongs, pulley systems and winches like the GRCS, plus rope, anchors and setup.
dek: How a rope puller for tree felling works, how it compares with come alongs, pulley systems and winches, and how to set one up safely.

sections.h: What a rope puller does in tree felling
p: A rope puller for tree felling puts steady, controlled tension on a pull line tied high in the tree. Used with a proper notch and hinge, that tension helps a tree go where you planned: it can take out some back lean, keep a tree from sitting back on the bar, and give you a margin of control when the target area is tight.

It is not a way to drag a tree against heavy lean or to fix a bad notch. The hinge still steers the tree. The puller adds force in the felling direction, and it lets one person on the ground apply that force in small, measured increments instead of guessing with a team pulling by hand.
Rope pullers, rope come alongs, endless rope winches and lever pullers are names for closely related tools. This guide covers how they differ and how to pick one that fits your work.

sections.h: Endless rope pullers vs cable come alongs
p: An endless or continuous rope puller grips the rope itself with a pair of jaws. Each stroke of the lever pulls the rope through, and the jaws hold it between strokes. Because it is not winding rope onto a drum, the pull length is limited only by the length of rope you have. The Maasdam continuous rope puller is the best-known example in tree work.

A cable come along winds steel cable onto a small drum. It is strong and compact, but the cable is short, so on a long pull you have to stop, re-rig and start again, which is the last thing you want with a tree half cut. That is why most arborists use a rope come along instead.

Whichever you use, check the rated capacity and the rope type and diameter the maker approves. A puller that slips on the wrong rope, or a rope that is weaker than the pull, turns a controlled job into an uncontrolled one.

A pulley system multiplies the force a person can put on the line. Fiddle block sets are a fast way to rig a simple mechanical advantage for pulling or tensioning, and a progress-capture pulley or rope grab lets you hold what you gain between pulls. Our mechanical advantage section has fiddle block sets and pulleys sized for rigging.

Real-world mechanical advantage is always lower than the theoretical number because of friction at each pulley and bend. Use rigging pulleys rather than carabiners at change-of-direction points, and keep the system simple enough that anyone on the crew can see how it is rigged.

Some lowering devices include a winch. The Good Rigging Control System (GRCS) is a trunk-mounted capstan with a winch that crews use for lowering, lifting and tensioning a pull line. If you already rig with a GRCS, it can double as a felling puller, anchored to a sound tree in the right direction.

Portable gas capstan winches are another option for heavy, repeated pulls. They are fast but need training, and the operator must be able to stop and hold the load at any moment. Pulling with a truck is a common cause of accidents because the driver cannot feel the tension and the load can change suddenly, so a hand-operated puller or a winch with a dedicated operator is the safer choice.

Use a low-stretch rigging rope for pulling. Stretchy rope stores energy and wastes your pulls. A double-braid line such as Samson Stable Braid is a common choice. Check the rope's strength, condition and the diameter range your puller accepts.

Run enough rope that the puller and the person working it sit well outside the fall zone. Many crews plan for a pull line at least one and a half to two times the height of the tree. Anchor the puller to a sound tree or other solid anchor with a rated sling, such as a whoopie or soft anchor sling, and tie the pull line as high in the tree as you safely can for better leverage.

Plan the fall, clear the area, cut the notch and agree on signals before anyone touches the puller. Most crews take up slack and set a moderate tension before the back cut, then add tension on the faller's call as the hinge forms. Over-tensioning before the cut can split the trunk or pull the tree before the hinge is ready.

Never stand in the bight of the rope or in line with a tensioned rope, which can snap back if something fails. Communication between the faller and the puller operator is everything. Learn these techniques from a qualified trainer, and follow ANSI Z133 and your company's procedures.
list: Plan the felling direction and escape routes
Anchor the puller outside the fall zone
Take up slack and set light tension before the back cut
Add tension only on the faller's call
Stay out of the bight and out of line with the rope

sections.h: How to choose a rope puller
p: For most tree services, a quality continuous rope puller, a dedicated length of low-stretch rigging rope, and a couple of anchor slings cover nearly every pull. Crews that already run a GRCS or a pulley system can use those for tensioning too.

Compare rated capacity, the rope diameters it accepts, handle length, weight on the carry, and whether replacement parts such as a replacement handle are easy to find. Keep the jaws clean and inspect the puller and rope before each job.

faq.q: What is an endless rope puller?
faq.a: A lever tool that grips the rope with jaws and pulls it through with each stroke. Because it does not wind rope onto a drum, the pull length is limited only by the rope you have.

faq.q: Can I use a cable come along to fell a tree?
faq.a: It can work for short pulls, but the short cable often means re-rigging mid-pull. Most arborists prefer a rope puller for felling.

faq.q: How long should a pull line be?
faq.a: Long enough that the puller and its operator are well outside the fall zone. Many crews plan for at least one and a half to two times the tree's height.

faq.q: Is the GRCS a winch?
faq.a: The GRCS is a lowering device with a built-in capstan winch, so crews also use it for lifting and tensioning a pull line.

title: Lowering Device for Tree Work: Port-a-Wrap to GRCS
h1: Choosing a Lowering Device for Tree Work
meta: How to choose a lowering device for tree work: Port-a-Wrap, Hobbs H2, GRCS and other friction devices, plus the bull rope, slings and blocks that go with them.
dek: How a lowering device for tree work controls rigged loads, how the main options compare, and the rope and hardware that complete the system.

sections.h: What a lowering device for tree work does
p: A lowering device for tree work is a friction device mounted at the base of the tree or on a nearby anchor. The rigging line runs from the load, up through a block or crotch in the tree, and down to the device, where it takes a number of wraps around a drum or post. The friction from those wraps lets one person on the ground hold, run and stop heavy pieces with a manageable amount of tail tension.

Without a lowering device, the ground worker is relying on gloves, a tree trunk and luck. With one, they can let a piece run, slow it, and stop it where it needs to land. It protects the groundie's hands, reduces wear on the rope and gives the crew far more control over where wood ends up.

Tree limb lowering devices range from a simple aluminum post to trunk-mounted capstans with built-in winches. The right choice depends on how heavy your rigging is and whether you also need to lift and tension.

The Port-a-Wrap is the classic friction lowering device: a post with horns that you attach to the trunk with a sling, chain or strap. You add friction by taking more wraps and control the load with tail tension. It is light, inexpensive and easy to learn, and it handles a large share of residential rigging.

Buckingham makes them in several sizes. The Port-A-Wrap Mini suits light rigging, the medium Portawrap is the everyday size for many crews, and the large model takes bigger rope and heavier loads. Kits like the Port-a-Wrap with a whoopie sling give you the device and an anchor sling together.
The main limitation is that a Port-a-Wrap is for lowering only. Adding or removing wraps under load is awkward, so set the number of wraps for the expected load before the cut.

The Hobbs H2 is a trunk-mounted lowering device with a drum that you take wraps around, like a Port-a-Wrap, but with a mechanism that lets the operator take in rope as well as let it out. Hobbs markets it as a lowering and lifting device, so crews use it to take up slack, pre-tension a rigging line and make small lifts.

It costs considerably more than a Port-a-Wrap and is heavier to carry, but it gives a level of control that many removal crews find worth it on heavy rigging jobs. Follow the maker's manual for rope size, number of wraps and working limits.

The Good Rigging Control System (GRCS) is a trunk-mounted capstan with a built-in winch, strapped to the tree. Crews use it to lower heavy pieces, lift loads, tension lines and pull trees over. It is one of the most capable tree rigging systems you can put on a trunk and one of the most expensive.

The Stein RCW 3001 is another heavy-duty trunk-mounted option, with an add-on winch kit. CMI's LCD and the Jail Brake are friction devices built for controlled lowering. For light rigging, a rigging rope wrench uses friction in a compact device, but stay within the load marked on it.
If you rig large wood every week, a winch-equipped device pays for itself in time and control. If most of your rigging is small to medium limbs, a Port-a-Wrap or similar friction device is plenty.

The rigging line, often called a bull rope, carries the load. Most arborists use a double-braid polyester rigging rope for its strength and low stretch. Popular choices include Samson Stable Braid, Samson Arbor-Plex, Teufelberger Sirius bull rope and Husky bull rope, in diameters such as 1/2, 5/8 and 3/4 inch.

Match the rope to your lowering device, block and slings. Every device has a rope diameter range, and running rope outside it can mean too little friction or too much heat and wear. Shock loads from a dropped piece can be many times the piece's weight, so plan rigging loads with a generous design factor, inspect rope before every job, and retire rope that is glazed, cut, or has been badly shock-loaded. See our rigging rope section for options.

sections.h: Slings, blocks and the rest of the system
p: A lowering device is only one part of the rigging system. At the top, a rigging block on a sling gives the line a smooth, rated redirect instead of grinding over a natural crotch. At the bottom, an anchor sling attaches the device to the trunk. Every connection in between needs to be rated for the load.

Adjustable whoopie slings, dead-eye slings and ring slings are the common choices. Our rigging slings and rigging blocks sections cover the main types. The system is only as strong as its weakest component.

sections.h: Matching a lowering device to your work
p: Think about the heaviest pieces you rig regularly, not the occasional giant, and the size of rope your crew already uses. Then decide whether you need lifting and tensioning or lowering alone.
list: Light pruning and small removals: Port-a-Wrap Mini or a rigging rope wrench
Everyday residential removals: medium or large Port-a-Wrap with an anchor sling
Heavy rigging with lifting or pre-tension: Hobbs H2
Heavy rigging, lifting, tensioning and pulling: GRCS or a similar winch-equipped device

p: Rigging puts large forces on people, trees and equipment. Learn it from a qualified trainer, and follow ANSI Z133, the manufacturer's instructions and your company's procedures. Agree on clear signals between the climber and the ground before any piece is cut.

Keep hands well clear of the wraps and the drum, wear gloves, and stand where a running line cannot catch you. Inspect the device, slings and rope before each job, and retire anything cracked, deformed or excessively worn.

faq.q: What is a Port-a-Wrap?
faq.a: A friction lowering device attached to the base of a tree. The rigging line takes wraps around it, and the ground worker controls the load with tail tension.

faq.q: What is the difference between a Port-a-Wrap and a GRCS?
faq.a: A Port-a-Wrap lowers loads only. The GRCS adds a capstan winch, so it can also lift, tension and pull, but it costs much more and weighs more.

faq.q: What size bull rope should I use with a lowering device?
faq.a: Use a rope within the diameter range the device maker specifies, and rated for your loads. Many crews use 1/2, 5/8 or 3/4 inch double-braid rigging rope.

faq.q: Is a Hobbs lowering device worth it?
faq.a: For crews that rig heavy wood often and want to take in rope or pre-tension lines, many find it worth the cost. For light rigging, a Port-a-Wrap is usually enough.

title: Arborist Clothing: Pants, Shirts and Brands That Last
h1: Arborist Clothing: What Tree Workers Actually Wear
meta: A practical guide to arborist clothing: climbing pants, chainsaw trousers like Arbortec BreatheFlex Pro, tree climbing shirts, boots, layers and top brands.
dek: Arborist clothing that holds up to climbing, rigging and brush work, from climbing pants and chainsaw trousers to shirts, boots and the brands crews trust.

sections.h: What arborist clothing needs to do
p: Arborist clothing takes more abuse than almost any other workwear. It scrapes on bark, catches on stubs, soaks up sweat on a hot climb, and has to move with you through every reach, step and knee-up into a crotch. Good tree work clothes stretch where you bend, resist abrasion where you rub, breathe when you sweat, and fit around a saddle without bunching.

It helps to separate two categories. Work clothing, like climbing pants and shirts, protects you from scrapes, sun and weather. Personal protective equipment, like chainsaw pants or chaps, is designed to stop a moving chain. Climbing pants are not cut protection, however tough they feel.
This guide covers both, plus boots, layers and the brands that tree crews tend to buy again.

Climbing pants are built for movement and abrasion. Look for a gusseted crotch, articulated or stretch knees, reinforced wear areas, and a waist that sits comfortably under a saddle belt. Pockets should not sit where leg loops or a lanyard will press on them.

Arborwear is the name many US climbers know best. The Original Tree Climbers' Pants are a heavy, durable classic, while the Ascender and Canopy pants are lighter for warm weather. Teufelberger's wayUP Light and Clogger's Spider pants are other popular climbing pants. Browse our climbing pants for the range.

sections.h: Chainsaw pants and the Arbortec BreatheFlex Pro
p: When you run a saw, your legs need cut-resistant protection. Chainsaw pants have layers of long fibers that pull into the sprocket and stop the chain, and many climbers prefer them to chaps because they move better and do not snag. We cover the trade-offs in chainsaw chaps vs chainsaw pants.

Arbortec is a UK brand, often searched as "arbortech pants" or "arbor tech pants". Its BreatheFlex Pro chainsaw trousers are popular with climbers for their stretch panels and ventilation, and they come in several colors, camo versions and protection types. Clogger, from Australia, is the other big name, with lines such as the Zero, DefenderPro and Ascend. See our chainsaw pants section to compare.
Check the label for the standard and protection type each pair meets, and make sure it matches what your work and employer require. Retire chainsaw pants after any cut into the protective layer.

The best tree climbing shirts are long-sleeved more often than not. Sleeves protect your arms from bark, poison ivy, insects and sun, and a lightweight wicking fabric keeps you cooler than bare skin on a summer climb. Choose a cut long enough to stay tucked under a saddle and with enough shoulder room to reach overhead.

For roadside work, wear high-visibility colors or a vest that meets your traffic control requirements. In cold weather, layer a wicking base, a fleece or a heavy hoodie like the Arborwear Double Thick, and a waterproof shell such as Arbortec's BreatheDry smock. Our sweatshirts and jackets section covers mid and outer layers.

sections.h: Boots for climbing and ground work
p: Boots are part of your arborist clothing and part of your PPE. Chainsaw boots, such as the Arbortec Scafell Lite, Arbortec Kayo and HAIX Protector models, add cut protection in the front of the foot for saw work. Spur climbers often choose a stiff, tall boot with a strong shank, like the Wesco Highliner, to support the foot on gaffs.
Fit matters more than features. A boot that fits well, supports your ankle and grips bark is safer than an expensive boot that hurts. See our arborist boots section for options.

sections.h: Arborist clothing brands at a glance
p: A handful of arborist clothing brands show up on most crews. Each has a slightly different focus, so it is common to mix them.
list: Arborwear: US brand known for durable climbing pants, Double Thick sweatshirts and work shirts
Arbortec: UK brand known for BreatheFlex Pro chainsaw trousers, jackets and chainsaw boots
Clogger: Australian brand focused on light, cool chainsaw pants and chaps
Teufelberger: Austrian rope maker that also makes climbing pants and technical layers
HAIX and Wesco: boot makers popular for chainsaw and spur-climbing boots

p: A thin helmet liner beanie or neck warmer keeps you warm under a helmet in winter without crowding the fit. Suspenders help keep heavier chainsaw pants up when your saddle belt is doing other work, and a low-profile webbing belt will not dig in under a saddle.
Gloves are worth buying in multiples: thin, grippy gloves for climbing and rope work, and heavier ones for brush and chipper duty. Our gloves section covers both.

Try climbing clothes on in a climbing position: knee high, arms overhead, and seated in a saddle if you can. Size for the layers you will wear underneath in cold weather. Wash chainsaw pants according to the label, since harsh cleaning can affect the protective layer, and repair small tears in work pants before they grow.
Replace clothing when it no longer protects you. Worn-through knees are a nuisance; a cut chainsaw pant is a hazard.

For a crew, it is worth setting a simple standard: chainsaw pants or chaps for anyone running a saw, long sleeves for climbers, and high-visibility layers for roadside jobs. Buying a couple of spare pairs of gloves and a backup layer for each truck saves a lost morning when someone shows up underdressed or soaked.

faq.q: What do arborists wear?
faq.a: Durable climbing pants or chainsaw pants, long-sleeved shirts, boots with good support, gloves, and a helmet with eye and hearing protection. High-visibility layers are added for roadside work.

faq.q: Are Arbortec and arbortech pants the same thing?
faq.a: Yes. The brand is Arbortec, a UK maker of arborist clothing. Arbortech and arbor tech are common misspellings.

faq.q: Do tree climbing pants protect against a chainsaw?
faq.a: No. Climbing pants resist abrasion but are not cut protection. Wear chainsaw pants or chaps when you run a saw.

faq.q: What are the best shirts for tree climbing?
faq.a: Lightweight, long-sleeved shirts in a wicking fabric, cut long enough to stay tucked under a saddle. Choose high-visibility colors for roadside work.

title: Husqvarna 330LK vs 525L: Which Trimmer to Buy
meta: Husqvarna 330LK vs 525L and 525LK compared: split shaft vs straight shaft, attachments, trimmer line size, fuel and which weed eater suits a tree crew best.
dek: The Husqvarna 330LK, 525L and 525LK compared the way a tree and landscape crew would use them, plus line size, fuel and attachments.

p: The Husqvarna 330LK and the 525L are both gas string trimmers with a loop handle, and both come up when crews shop for a dependable weed eater for cleanup around jobs. The key difference is the shaft. The 330LK has a split, detachable shaft that accepts attachments. The 525L has a one-piece straight shaft and is a dedicated trimmer.

The 525L belongs to Husqvarna's 525 professional series, with a 25.4 cc X-Torq engine. There is also a 525LK, which pairs that same 25.4 cc engine with a split shaft, so it is the professional-series answer to the 330LK. If you want attachments, you are choosing between the 330LK and the 525LK. If you want a straight trimmer, the 525L is the one.
For model details, see the Husqvarna 330LK, Husqvarna 525L and Husqvarna 525LK pages.

The 525 series is built for daily professional use, and its X-Torq engine is designed to reduce fuel use and emissions compared with older two-stroke designs. It is a light, quick-revving engine that suits long days of trimming along fences, beds and job-site edges.

The 330LK is aimed at buyers who want a capable combi power head at a lower price. Check the current Husqvarna spec sheet for its exact engine figures before you buy, since specifications can change between production years and markets.

A split shaft lets one engine drive several tools. With a combi power head like the 330LK or 525LK, you can swap the trimmer for attachments such as an edger, hedge trimmer, pole saw, cultivator or blower, provided they are listed as compatible. For a small crew or a homeowner with a lot of property, that saves buying and maintaining several engines.

A straight shaft like the 525L's is a little simpler and more rigid, with nothing to loosen or wear at the coupling. Crews that trim all day and already own dedicated edgers and hedge trimmers often prefer it.

For a tree crew, the deciding question is usually what else you need the engine to do. A split-shaft power head with a pole saw attachment can handle light clearance pruning around a job, then switch back to a trimmer for cleanup. A dedicated pole saw or trimmer is faster for heavy, repeated use, so think about how many hours each tool will really run.

If you are searching for a 525LK brush cutter attachment, check the manual for approved cutting attachments. Fitting a brush blade usually requires the right guard, and often a different handle and a harness. Never fit a blade to a trimmer that is not approved for it.

sections.h: Trimmer line size for the 330LK and 525L
p: One of the most common questions about the Husqvarna 330LK is what string size it takes. The right answer is in the operator's manual and on the trimmer head itself, which is marked or documented with the line diameter range it accepts. Heads can differ between model years and replacement heads, so check the head on your machine rather than going by someone else's.

Running thicker line than the head is rated for overloads the engine and clutch and makes the line harder to feed. Thinner line wears faster. Husqvarna sells round and shaped lines such as Titanium X-Pro and TrimForce in several diameters, so you can match the size in your manual.

Both trimmers are loop-handle models, which are compact and easy to move around obstacles but put more strain on your arms over a long day than a bike-handle trimmer with a harness. A shoulder strap helps on long runs.

If you landed here searching for T525 weight, that is a different tool: the Husqvarna T525 is a small top-handle chainsaw weighing about 5.9 lb as a power head, designed for trained arborists working in trees.

Both trimmers run on a gas and two-stroke oil mix. Husqvarna specifies 50:1 for its two-stroke engines; check your manual and use fresh fuel. Premixed fuel such as Husqvarna 50:1 premix avoids mixing errors and keeps well in storage.

Clean the air filter often in dusty conditions, check the spark plug, keep the cooling fins clear, and grease the gearhead at the intervals in the manual. On combi models, keep the coupling clean and fully tightened.
list: Use fresh 50:1 fuel or premix
Clean the air filter regularly
Check the spark plug and cooling fins
Grease the gearhead as the manual specifies
Use only the line size and attachments approved for your model

p: Pick the 525L if you want a dedicated professional trimmer that runs all day and you already own other tools for edging and hedges. Pick the 525LK if you want the same professional engine with the flexibility of attachments. Pick the 330LK if you want combi flexibility at a lower price and your trimming is more occasional.
Whatever you choose, wear eye protection, hearing protection, long pants and sturdy boots when trimming, and keep bystanders well back from the head.

faq.q: What string size does the Husqvarna 330LK use?
faq.a: Check the operator's manual and the trimmer head on your machine for the line diameter range it accepts, since heads can vary by model year and replacement head.

faq.q: Is the Husqvarna 525L a professional trimmer?
faq.a: Yes. It is part of Husqvarna's 525 professional series, with a 25.4 cc X-Torq engine and a straight shaft.

faq.q: Can I put attachments on a 525L?
faq.a: No. The 525L has a one-piece straight shaft. The 525LK and 330LK have split shafts that accept compatible attachments.

faq.q: How much does a Husqvarna T525 weigh?
faq.a: The T525 top-handle chainsaw weighs about 5.9 lb as a power head, before bar, chain and fuel.

title: Arborist Supplies: What a Tree Care Business Needs
h1: Arborist Supplies: A Checklist for Every Role on the Crew
meta: An arborist supplies checklist by role: climber, rigging, saws, ground crew, PPE and plant health care, with links to compare tree care gear and typical prices.
dek: The arborist supplies a tree care business needs, organized by who uses them, with links to compare gear in each category.

sections.h: How to use this arborist supplies checklist
p: Arborist supplies cover everything from a climber's saddle to chipper knives and traffic cones. This checklist groups them by role on a typical tree crew: climber, rigging, saws, ground crew, safety and plant health care. Use it to equip a new crew, fill gaps in an existing one, or plan what to replace next season.

Gap Arborist Supply is an independent online buying guide, not a physical store. We show typical prices and send you to retailers to check current prices and buy. If you are searching for an arborist supply store near you, a local dealer is still the best place for saw service and fitting boots, but comparing gear online first helps you walk in knowing what you want.
Each section below links to the relevant category so you can compare products, and to our more detailed guides where we have them.

The climber's kit is life-support equipment, and it is where quality matters most. A saddle, climbing rope, friction hitch or mechanical device, lanyard, carabiners, helmet and throw line make up the core. We walk through each piece in detail, from first kit to professional setup, in our tree climbing gear checklist.

For a business, plan on spares: a second climbing line for each climber, extra hitch cords and carabiners, and replacement parts for saddles and spurs. Start with our climbing section, and see climbing rope and saddles and harnesses for the two biggest purchases. All life-support gear must meet ANSI Z133 requirements and be used as the manufacturer instructs.

Tree rigging equipment lets you take down wood in controlled pieces instead of dropping it. The basics are rigging rope, slings, a rigging block and a lowering device at the base. Crews doing heavier removals add more blocks, rings, a winch-equipped device and mechanical advantage for lifting and pulling.

Browse rigging rope, rigging slings, blocks and hardware and lowering devices. Our lowering device guide compares the Port-a-Wrap, Hobbs H2 and GRCS, and our rope puller guide covers pulling and tensioning for felling.
list: Bull rope sized for your blocks and lowering device
Anchor and block slings, such as whoopie and dead-eye slings
Rigging blocks and rings
A friction lowering device
A rope puller or mechanical advantage kit for felling pulls

p: Most tree services run a range of saws: a top-handle for the climber, a mid-size saw for limbing and brush, a 70 cc saw for removals and a larger saw for the biggest wood. See our chainsaws section and the biggest Husqvarna chainsaw guide for how the sizes compare.

Saws need a steady supply of bars and chain, files, fuel, bar oil and replacement parts. For hand tools, every climber needs a pruning saw, and the crew needs pole saws and pruners for clearance and finish work. See cutting and pruning and our pole saw guide.

sections.h: Ground crew and tree felling equipment
p: The ground crew moves the most wood and needs tools that survive it. Felling wedges and an axe or maul, a felling bar or cant hook, and log handling tools such as tongs and pickaroons make bucking and loading faster and easier on backs.

Look at felling wedges, logging tools and landscaper tools for rakes and cleanup gear. If you run your own chipper and grinder, keep spare chipper knives and stump grinder teeth on hand so a dull set does not end the day early.

Every person on the crew needs a helmet, eye protection, hearing protection, gloves and boots, plus chainsaw pants or chaps for anyone who runs a saw. Our safety section covers each, and chainsaw chaps vs chainsaw pants explains the leg protection choice.

Beyond personal gear, each truck should carry a stocked first aid kit with bleeding control, traffic control signs and cones for roadside work, and a reliable way for the climber and ground to talk, such as helmet radios. Crews with bucket trucks need fall protection for aerial lifts and, often, ground protection mats.

sections.h: Plant health care, cabling and planting
p: Many tree services also offer cabling, bracing and planting. Cabling work needs cable or synthetic systems, eye bolts or lags, and the tools to install them correctly. Planting jobs need staking and support materials and sometimes earth anchors.
See cabling and bracing and planting. Follow the current ANSI A300 standards and the manufacturer's instructions for any support system you install.

sections.h: Buying arborist supplies for a crew
p: If you are equipping several crews, standardize where you can. Matching rope diameters, carabiner types, saw models and bar and chain sizes means fewer parts to stock and fewer mistakes on the truck. Keep an inspection log for life-support and rigging gear, and budget to retire it on schedule rather than when it fails.

If you buy in volume, ask retailers about commercial or wholesale pricing on consumables. Typical prices on this site are a guide to what a buyer would see, not a quote, so check the retailer for current pricing.
list: Saw chain, bars, files and fuel
Hitch cords, carabiners and slings that wear out
Gloves, earplugs and eye protection
First aid restocks
Chipper knives and grinder teeth

faq.q: Where can I buy arborist supplies?
faq.a: This site is an independent online buying guide. We list typical prices and link to retailers where you can check current prices and buy. Local dealers are useful for saw service and fitting.

faq.q: Can I buy wholesale arborist supplies?
faq.a: Many retailers offer commercial or volume pricing to tree care businesses, especially on consumables. Ask the retailer directly.

faq.q: What arborist supplies does a new tree service need first?
faq.a: Climbing gear for each climber, a basic rigging kit with rope, slings, a block and a lowering device, a range of chainsaws, PPE for everyone, and a first aid kit on every truck.

faq.q: What is the difference between climbing gear and rigging equipment?
faq.a: Climbing gear supports the climber and is life-support equipment. Rigging equipment controls the wood being cut and lowered. Do not mix the two.
